data.title: Supreme Court to tackle AR-15 bans in blockbuster 2nd Amendment case
data.description:

Fourteen years after a lone gunman carried out the deadliest elementary school shooting in American history, the Supreme Court is turning to a bitter legal fight over whether communities may outlaw the type of weapon used in that massacre — a popular class of semi-automatic guns that includes the AR-15.

In one of the most notable Second Amendment cases to reach the 6-3 conservative court in decades, the justices will hear arguments Wednesday over state and local bans on “assault-style” weapons, such as the AR-15, some of which were enacted or strengthened in response to a dramatic increase in mass shootings since 20 first graders and six educators were killed in 2012 at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut.

For the government officials and gun safety groups defending the bans, the memory of deadly shootings involving the AR-15 is a driving force.

“The basic function of government is to keep its citizenry safe, and these guns are so incredibly dangerous in a densely populated area like Chicago,” said Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, a Democrat, who is defending one of the bans at the Supreme Court. “One hundred percent of the children who were hit with this weapon at Sandy Hook died.”

But two trends have emerged in recent years that benefit gun rights groups. First, far more Americans own an AR-15 today — as many as 26 million people, according to one estimate — than even a decade ago. The Supreme Court acknowledged as much last year, noting in a unanimous opinion that the weapons are “widely legal,” purchased by “many ordinary consumers” and that the AR–15 “is the most popular rifle in the country.”

Second, the court’s conservatives has quickly and vastly expanded the scope and meaning of the Second Amendment.

In a series of landmark decisions, the court found for the first time that the Constitution provides individual Americans a right to own a handgun at home and to carry that weapon outside. It has made it easier to bring guns onto private property open to the public, such as stores. It has required governments defending gun laws to find a “historical antecedent,” a similar rule on the books when the Second Amendment was ratified in 1791.

In a 2008 decision that gun rights groups will cite heavily during arguments this week, the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia suggested that the Second Amendment protects weapons that are in “common use.” The plaintiffs challenging the AR-15 bans in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, use the phrase “common use” 56 times in their main brief supporting their position.

Twenty-seven wooden angel figures stand in a wooded area beside a road, in Newtown, Connecticut, on December 16, 2012, following the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School.

The Trump administration, which is backing the gun rights groups, used that phrase 49 times in its own brief filed in September.

Kostas Moros, director of legal research and education at the Second Amendment Foundation, acknowledged that AR-15s are dangerous. But he noted that all firearms are dangerous — and, despite that, the framers protected Americans’ ability to own them in the Constitution.

“They gave the people the uninfringeable right to keep and bear arms, and that is a right of the people — not of the states, not of the government — to decide,” Moros said.

Dangerous and unusual

Blockbuster appeals at the Supreme Court are often complicated. The case over AR-15 bans, by contrast, is relatively straightforward.

Connecticut and Cook County are leaning into the Supreme Court’s reasoning in a 2022 precedent, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, which struck down a strict requirement in New York that residents show cause to obtain a carry permit. As part of that decision, a 6-3 majority concluded that in order to survive a Second Amendment challenge, modern-day gun regulations needed to have some grounding in the “nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

While the court has tinkered with that standard in subsequent decisions, the state and county say there is an extensive history — dating to medieval times — of English laws banning especially dangerous weapons. Their briefs spend considerable ink discussing bans on crossbows and certain lances.

“From fourteenth-century England to twenty-first century America, governments have restricted weapons because of their unusually dangerous properties,” Connecticut officials told the Supreme Court this fall. “In each instance, legislatures have determined that a weapon is atypically lethal relative to its peers — and so have acted to prevent that weapon’s use.”

Thomas, who wrote the majority opinion in Bruen, seemed to dismiss the relevance of some of that same history when it came to handguns, noting that one of those laws came “more than 200 years before the birth of Shakespeare, more than 350 years before the Salem Witch Trials.” But he flicked at the idea that banning “launcegays” may have made sense given that they were carried when “one intended to engage in lawful combat.”

Supporters of the ban see that logic as a potential opening.

Connecticut and Cook County — which includes Chicago — note the AR-15’s ties to its military counterpart, the M16. They note that AR-15s, like other long guns, are more accurate than handguns. The weapons, which first came onto the commercial market in the 1960s, can feature a bullet that tumbles on its axis when it hits a target, creating more significant wounds, the state and county said. The weapon’s design limits recoil more than many hunting rifles, allowing a shooter to maintain control even during rapid, semi-automatic firing.

Burke, the Cook County prosecutor, said the weapon’s range and design make it “unbelievably dangerous for law enforcement.”

“It was designed for the military,” she said. “It was designed to take out enemy combatants at the greatest distance possible.”

A bullet impact crater is seen in concrete, after a gunman opened fire with an AR-15 at the Edmund Burke School in Washington, DC, on on April 28, 2022.

Gun rights groups focus first on the weapon’s popularity.

Only 11 states have approved bans on AR-15s, and so the rifles are widely available and in use by gun owners across the country, the vast majority of whom never commit a crime. The plaintiffs challenging the bans described the AR-15 as the “paradigmatic American rifle” in written arguments. According to one survey, roughly 30% of American gun owners have an AR-15 or similar rifle, which works out to 26 million people. A Washington Post-Ipsos survey from 2022 works out to about 16 million Americans.

Those numbers alone, the plaintiffs said, should resolve the case in their favor.

Scalia’s 2008 precedent in District of Columbia v. Heller “stands for the proposition that arms in common use cannot be banned,” the plaintiffs told the justices.

The challengers also reject the idea that an AR-15 is more dangerous than other guns. They argue that the caliber most often used is smaller than that of many traditional hunting rifles. And they scoff at some of the warnings from government officials as bordering on science fiction.

“These are ordinary rifles,” the plaintiffs told the justices in one brief, “not phasers from Star Trek.”

“If a madman was going to my daughter’s school, I wouldn’t feel much better if he quote-unquote only had a Glock, versus an AR-15,” said Moros, whose group is one of the plaintiffs challenging the bans. “My theory has always been, you need to make targets less vulnerable to attack, rather than worry so much about what the particular gun does.”

Counting to five

Connecticut and Cook County face headwinds for another reason: At least four conservative justices have signaled skepticism with the bans to varying degrees. If that holds, it means the government will need to find at least two justices to reach a five-vote majority, assuming the court’s three-justice liberal wing supports them.

Justice Clarence Thomas, among the court’s most stalwart conservatives, made clear in 2015 that he felt lower courts upholding the bans were “relegating the Second Amendment to a second-class right.” A year later, in a case involving stun guns, Justice Samuel Alito wrote that “the relative dangerousness of a weapon is irrelevant when the weapon belongs to a class of arms commonly used for lawful purposes.” Justice Neil Gorsuch has been less clear, though he voted last year to hear a similar case dealing with Maryland’s AR-15 ban.

Associate Supreme Court Justices Samuel Alito, Jr., Clarence Thomas and Brett Kavanaugh attend President Donald Trump's second inauguration, in the Rotunda of the US Capitol on January 20, 2025.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative who is closer to the center than Alito or Thomas, wrote in the Maryland case that the state was “something of an outlier” by having a ban on the weapons. And, he said, given that millions of Americans own one, the challengers had a “strong argument” that AR-15s are protected by the Second Amendment. As an appeals court judge in 2011, Kavanaugh also dissented from a decision upholding a Washington, DC, ban on “assault-style” rifles.

If that holds, it means there will be an enormous amount of focus on Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett at the arguments Wednesday.

Still, groups that support additional gun regulations say they’re optimistic about the appeal. The earlier cases dealt with handguns, they note, which are more commonly used for home defense. And most federal appeals courts to review the laws — including the 7th Circuit in the Cook County case and the 2nd Circuit in the Connecticut dispute — upheld the laws.

“The chief and Justice Barrett have articulated a history-based test that looks for something useful in the history. It doesn’t just look for a Constitution frozen in time. It looks for a way in which the Constitution can still have relevance,” said Billy Clark, associate litigation director at the Giffords Law Center.

The chief justice, Clark said, is “someone who recognizes the consequences” of the court’s decisions, and “I think is going to be cautious about saying that these sorts of weapons are constitutionally enshrined.”

data.title: More than 600,000 still without power after Thanksgiving storms batter both coasts
data.description:
U.S.

Powerful Thanksgiving Day storm brings flooding, power outages to Northeast, Midwest

Updated on: November 27, 2026 / 1:04 PM EST / CBS/AP

Add CBS News on Google

A Thanksgiving storm brought foul weather to the East Coast and Midwest on Thursday, causing major power outages, disrupting holiday travel and prompting the historic postponement of New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

More than 500,000 customers were without power Friday afternoon across the Midwest and Northeast, according to the utility tracking website PowerOutage.us. Of those, more than 122,000 customers were without electricity in Pennsylvania, along with more than 92,000 in New Jersey and 66,000 in Maryland. The outages reached more than 800,000 customers at the height of the storm Thursday night.

There were 1,673 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday midday, with another 119 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. But that is a far cry from the more than 2,500 flights to or from U.S. destinations delayed on Thursday, while more than 460 were canceled, according to FlightAware.

The storm hammered sections of the East Coast with torrential rain, high winds and flooding. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, declared by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Wednesday night, as were parts of New York, following a declaration from Gov. Kathy Hochul. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.

Stormy weather creates havoc in New York City

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning that two people had to be rescued from their cars because of flooding. He cautioned people not to attempt to walk, bike or drive through flooded areas.

"We want to remind everyone to stay safe and there is no destination worth your safety," Mamdani said.

The New York City Emergency Management agency reported that the city received 1.5 to 2 inches of rain on Thanksgiving, with some parts seeing up to 3 inches. High tides brought flooding to the city's coastal areas, including portions of Staten Island and Long Island.

Central Park saw wind gusts higher than 30 mph, the agency said, while LaGuardia Airport recorded winds of 56 mph. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, with no injuries were reported.  

Macy's postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade's massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.

A high school marching band from Pearland, Texas, near Houston, said it raised a staggering $350,000 to allow its 500 members to stay in New York City for two extra nights.

"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band for Pearland High School, told CBS News on Thursday.

Visitors who had traveled to New York to attend the parade were forced to make last-minute changes to their travel plans. Amanda Anderson, a Florida-based makeup artist who was hired to do makeup for parade performers, told CBS News New York she was able to rebook her flights so she could stay an extra day.

"I was in Macy's, actually, when I found out, and I look up and there was like three girls crying already," Anderson said when she learned the parade had been postponed. "People were sitting down, very somber. It was an experience."

Major roadways flooded, holiday travel disrupted

The storm flooded coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in Thursday morning. Roads were closed and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.

Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said.

"Not quite Hurricane Sandy," Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south of New Jersey's Atlantic coast.

Floodwaters washed debris over the road next to the shore, and a few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

Lance Miller, 54, said floods in his neighborhood of Ocean City, a small coastal town in New Jersey, are about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest grocery store would probably "destroy your car."

"I wouldn't do that, I'm a car guy," said Miller. "You're gonna have a good foot of water that you'd have to drive through." 

Miller, who had his Thanksgiving Day meal preparations set, said he would be staying indoors and have dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends in the area were "not so lucky" and had flooding inside their homes.

"So they're dealing with cleanup, you know," he said.

The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted a video on Facebook of water pouring through the city's streets on a gray day even before heavy rains started.

A firefighter there said the tide was coming in ferociously and it was still an hour before its peak. Water closed in on steps to houses, and businesses had sandbags piled in front of their doors.

A stretch of U.S. Route 30, a major artery that goes into Atlantic City, was shuttered in both directions due to heavy flooding, the Absecon Police Department reported.

"Please stay off the roads until conditions improve," Absecon police said. "Do not attempt to drive through flooded roadways or around barricades."

Chester County Hospital in West Chester, Pennsylvania, sustained a partial power outage on Thursday afternoon, but power was restored before patients had to be transported to other facilities.

Residents of the Pennsylvania community of Springfield Township north of Philadelphia were asked to temporarily evacuate out of caution after a tree fell on a propane tank, local officials said. That evacuation advisory was later lifted.

The storm prompted the temporary closure of some coastal highways and bridges. The nearly 18-mile Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel over the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway.

North Carolina was particularly hard-hit by heavy rain. Emerald Isle, in the state's Outer Banks, received 9.16 inches of rain. Atlantic Beach, North Carolina, saw 9.06 inches.

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, which are in the Washington metropolitan area, were asked to conserve water by the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. The water conservation request, which applied to all 1.9 million WSSC customers, was due to the risk that power outages posed to the agency's two water filtration plants.

Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches of snowfall. French Village, Missouri, received 15 inches of show while Ste. Genevieve recorded 14 inches.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city.

The rain isn't quite over yet for the Northeast. More storms are expected Sunday night into Monday morning for New York City, Philadelphia and Boston.

data.title: Thanksgiving storms cause over 1 million power outages and disrupt East Coast travel
data.description:
WEATHER
National Weather Service

Powerful Thanksgiving storms knockout power, disrupt East Coast travel

Trevor Hughes BrieAnna J. Frank
USA TODAY
Updated Nov. 26, 2026, 11:04 p.m. ET

For millions of people around the country, Thanksgiving 2026 brought travel headaches, powerful storms and power outages.

Forecasters with the National Weather Service said poor weather was expected through Nov. 27 for much of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Travelers taking to the roads and skies were advised to check conditions.

"Heavy rain, damaging winds, and coastal flooding will continue through the afternoon and evening hours across portions of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast leading to moderate to major impacts over the region," the weather service said in an afternoon forecast. "Coastal flooding is ongoing across much of the Mid-Atlantic coast."

Earlier on Nov. 26, the storm stretched from St. Louis east to New York City and Boston, as far south as Nashville, and was closing in on Buffalo, New York. AAA projected 81.5 million people would travel at least 50 miles from home during the holiday period.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a preemptive state of emergency for New York City, and Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties. In New York City, gusts reached 40 mph.

Heavy Thanksgiving snow pounds Missouri

Parts of southeastern Missouri saw as much as 14 inches of snow between Nov. 25 and Thanksgiving morning, according to the National Weather Service in St. Louis. More than two inches of snow fell in Columbia, Missouri, with the weather service reporting it was the snowiest Thanksgiving morning in the city in more than two decades and the "biggest Thanksgiving snowstorm" in nearly 50 years.

St. Louis saw more than seven inches of snow, an increase from a 6.4-inch snowfall in 2025, the weather service said. It marks the first time on record that the city has "recorded a top 10 November snowfall in back to back years."

The Wentzville Ice Arena, northwest of St. Louis, collapsed in the storm and will remain closed "until further notice," officials said.

Over 800,000 power outages reported across US

USA TODAY's power outage tracker showed growing power losses in coastal Virginia, particularly around Newport News and Williamsburg, and also in St. Louis and the surrounding suburbs. Videos posted to social media showed street flooding in parts of eastern Virginia.

More than 800,000 power outages had been reported nationwide as of 10:46 p.m. ET, largely centered in Missouri and the East Coast. In Maryland, officials closed the Bay Bridge to travel in both directions, and live traffic cameras bounced in the wind and rain.

Storm affecting Maryland water treatment plants

The Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission asked nearly two million customers in Maryland's Montgomery and Prince George's counties to "immediately conserve water" because the storm was causing "intermittent power disruptions" at water treatment plants in the Washington metro area.

The commission asked residents to use water only for essential purposes to "preserve water for fire protection and system storage." In a 6 p.m. ET update, the commission said the request remained in effect throughout both counties.

Both the Potomac and Patuxent water filtration plants had power and were producing drinking water at that time, the commission said, adding that they may still "experience storm-related interruptions."

The commission asked residents to take measures including taking shorter showers and limiting use of washing machines and dishwashers. Taking such measures "could help preserve water for system storage and fire protection until the storm passes and power reliability is restored," the statement said.

Landspout tornado possible southeast of Seattle

The National Weather Service in Seattle said Thanksgiving afternoon that a landspout tornado and penny-sized hail were possible in areas southeast of Seattle, including Auburn, Palmer and Cedar Falls.

The weather service's statement was set to expire at 1:45 p.m. local time.

A tornado warning was issued earlier to areas including Issaquah and North Bend, Washington.

Macy's parade rescheduled for Nov. 28

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged both residents and visitors alike to be safe as the storm approached the Big Apple. The Macy's parade was rescheduled to 8:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 28. The parade's delay set off a scramble for high school bands and other performers to find places to stay during the year's busiest travel period.

As of 3 p.m. ET, winds in Central Park were 20 mph with gusts of 41 mph, the weather service reported. Winds were expected to strengthen later in the day, with gusts of up to 65 mph. The weather service predicted "widespread" power outages and said high-profile vehicles could get blown over.

Parade organizers cited the poor weather in delaying the parade by two days, noting the popular large-scale balloons could pose a risk to handlers and crowds in high winds.

"If you are planning to travel, budget extra time and remember that no destination is worth your safety," Mamdani said in a social media post. "Never walk or drive through flooding. If winds pick up, go inside. These are winds strong enough to down tree limbs and power lines — so be sure to secure outdoor furniture, trash cans, and holiday decorations ahead of time."

Air travelers facing delays, cancellations

Most airlines issued travel waivers to passengers and reminded flyers to check for delays and cancellations.

As of 8 p.m. ET, there were 2,295 delays and 1,207 cancellations for U.S. flights, according to FlightAware's Misery Map. Baltimore/Washington International Airport had the most cancellations at that time, with 48 outbound and 46 inbound flights cancelled.

JFK International in New York, Boston's Logan International, and Miami International were also suffering significant delays and cancellations, according to FlightAware. Washington Dulles International Airport was experiencing departure delays averaging more than one hour as of 8 p.m. ET.

Department of Transportation rules require airlines to offer travelers a refund if their flight is canceled for any reason, regardless of ticket type, if they choose not to fly. If they choose to continue their trip, they are entitled to penalty-free rebooking on the same airline.

If a cancellation is outside of the airline's control – as is the case with inclement weather – the only thing travelers are owed is rebooking or a refund.

Concerns over California flooding

In California, dangerous coastal conditions persisted. The weather service warned of moderate to major coastal flooding in the San Francisco area, with a risk of unexpected "sneaker" waves of 13-19 feet high in some areas.

The weather service said people in the San Francisco area should expect some road closures and flooding of low-lying areas through 4 p.m. Pacific Time. A portion of the Pacifica Pier near San Francisco collapsed as it was battered by high waves on Nov. 25.

data.title: Ukraine says it downed a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time
data.description:
World

Ukraine says it has intercepted a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time

By
Mariia Kashchenko
Desk Editor
Mariia Kashchenko is News Desk Editor at the CBS News London Bureau. Mariia covers breaking news with a focus on the war in Ukraine and international affairs.
Read Full Bio
Mariia Kashchenko

November 26, 2026 / 7:02 AM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, marking a potentially significant development in the country's effort to defend cities from Russia's daily aerial attacks. 

The interception was carried out using the Blysk laser air defense system, which was developed and manufactured by Ukrainian defense technology firm Carmine Sky. Technology for laser air defense systems is being developed as part of the wider Private Air Defense program, Zelenskyy's adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said in a statement. 

About 100 companies across Ukraine have joined the government-backed private air defense initiative.

Russia started deploying jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine earlier this year. The weapons travel faster, making them harder to intercept than the more common propeller-driven attack drones. 

In June, Ukraine was only intercepting about 57% of the jet-powered drones, reflecting a significant vulnerability as Ukrainian forces had been shooting down about 90% of the conventional Russian attack drones. 

Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.

The laser interception reported by Beskrestnov this week gives some insight into Ukraine's mounting efforts to adapt both its offenses and defenses as Russia's weapons and tactics evolve.

Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line. 

Ukraine started testing laser air defense systems over the summer. According to Beskrestnov, the Blysk system was used to protect critical infrastructure, though he declined to give more specifics. 

He said a number of Ukrainian companies, including Carmine Sky, are working to develop laser technology, but he cautioned that "it is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser."

"Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he said.

data.title: Trump calls GDP figures 'fake' and demands investigation of Commerce Department
data.description:
Trump calls the pre-election GDP figures 'fake' and demands an investigation of Commerce Department

JOSH BOAK
Updated Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:08 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 2
President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump disembark Air Force One at Palm Beach International Airport, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, in West Palm Beach, Fla. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections, and said he wants to launch an investigation.

Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.

His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%.

Advertisement

The department's Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.

But the president claimed on social media that it was a "massive, and purposeful, error" and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.

"It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers," Trump posted. "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation."

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

It's the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavorable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated. In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported.

Trump called that jobs report "phony" and "rigged."

Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president's belief that the economy is strong. In the midterms, 76% described economic conditions as "not so good" or "poor," according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation.

The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation — the personal consumption expenditures price index — accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8% in October.

data.title: Heavy rains, winds and king tides batter coastal areas as 70 million face flood risks
data.description:
Live

Thanksgiving storms live updates: Heavy rains, winds and king tides batter coastal areas; 70 million face flooding; Macy's parade postponed due to weather

Travelers flocked to airports, roads and railways for one of the year's busiest travel days, with many facing rainstorms on the East Coast and coastal flooding in the West.

Jasmine Andersson, Harriet Sinclair
Updated Thu, November 26, 2026 at 12:42 PM UTC
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Stormy weather continues to hit both the East and West coasts, with more than 70 million people facing flood warnings and advisories and wind, gale and storm warnings in place on both sides of the country.

Thanksgiving travelers are likely to see delays, with road closures, detours and flight delays expected as the bad weather continues to roil transport.

According to AccuWeather, flood warnings, gale warnings and storm warnings are in place for a huge swath of the East coast, while coastal flood warnings are in place on much of California's coast. A total of 77.7 million people are living in areas that are under wind alerts, while more than 70 million are facing flood warnings and advisories.

Advertisement

There were 405 flight delays and 357 cancellations by 7.30 a.m. ET, according to FlightAware. This follows more than 1,000 delays Wednesday as travelers attempted to make their way across the country to celebrate Thanksgiving.

In New York, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed until Saturday, with the city expecting wind gusts of 30 to 45 mph today, while California has been battling surging king tides with an entire section of the Pacifica Pier demolished by waves Wednesday.

Florida has been buffered by a separate storm system that had led to flooding and road closures and is set to move up to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

Five states — Missouri, Illinois, Montana, Washington and Alaska — are under a winter storm warning, with some areas of the states expecting heavy snow and gusty winds that could lead to road closures and potential power line issues.

The National Weather Service has issued a coastal flood warning for the Pacific Coast and bay shorelines along San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay, while outside of Orlando, flooding has led to a number of road closures.

Live7 updates
    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 12:42 PM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      Is New York under a state of emergency? What to know as the Thanksgiving storm hits

      New York state Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Wednesday for New York City and Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties as a powerful Thanksgiving storm moves up the East Coast.

      The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for the city and Long Island from 10 a.m. Thursday until early Friday, with gusts of up to 60 mph forecast. Heavy rain and widespread coastal flooding are also expected, with the worst conditions arriving Thursday afternoon into the evening.

      "We're expecting heavy rain and strong winds that could create dangerous travel conditions," Hochul wrote on X.

      The MTA is banning empty tractor-trailers and tandem trucks from its bridges and tunnels from noon Thursday through at least midnight Friday, Hochul's statement said.

      The governor has urged people to allow extra time for travel and to text their county or borough name to 333111 for real-time weather alerts.

      The governor's office said about 5,780 utility workers are available statewide to respond to outages.

      New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill also declared a state of emergency for her state on Wednesday.

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 12:19 PM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      Winter storm warnings in the Midwest

      In the Midwest, a winter storm warning remains in effect Thanksgiving Day morning for St. Louis and surrounding parts of Missouri and Illinois, where the National Weather Service said heavy, wet snow was making roads slippery and holiday travel difficult.

      Up to 2 more inches were forecast through noon local time in the St. Louis area, with 2 to 4 more inches in parts of southeast Missouri, where the weight of the snow could also bring down power lines. Up to 13 inches (33 centimeters) of snow are expected in the St. Louis area by Thursday afternoon.

      Parts of western Illinois were downgraded to a winter weather advisory.

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 11:27 AM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      What are the National Weather Service's key messages for the East Coast today?

      The National Weather Service set out its key messages for the Thanksgiving storm moving up the East Coast, warning of major coastal flooding, strong winds and heavy rain moving into Thanksgiving Day.

      According to the latest available advisory, people should look out for:

      Coastal flooding. Moderate to major flooding is expected from Georgia to the Northeast into Thursday, driven by strong onshore winds, high surf and high astronomical tides. The greatest impacts are forecast along the Mid-Atlantic coast, from the Outer Banks to New Jersey.

      Wind. Gusts of 50 mph or more are forecast along the coast, and 45 mph or more inland to the I-95 corridor and the central Appalachians. Scattered power outages and tree damage are likely.

      Rain. Soaking rain is expected from the Southeast northward through southern New England, with 1 to 4 inches across the Mid-Atlantic and locally more along the North Carolina coast. Southern New England could see 1 to 2 inches.

      The agency urged people to monitor its forecasts and heed local officials.

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 11:15 AM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      Punishing king tides destroy Pacifica pier

      A video has captured the moment an entire section of California's Pacifica Pier was destroyed by king tides on Wednesday.

      The footage shows a massive wave tearing the end of the pier away and slamming it into the ocean, as powerful surf pounded the coastline.

      Officials had closed the L-shaped, 1,140 feet-long (350 meters-long) pier in the summer after finding cracks in the structure, the Associated Press reported.

      Beachfront homes in Pacifica, just south of San Francisco, started flooding earlier this week as the year's highest tides, known as king tides, rolled in.

      To the north, Marin County officials told residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach to prepare to evacuate, warning that large waves through the afternoon could push water and debris into roads and homes. That warning was later lifted, but people were still urged to keep away from the beach as heavy surf continued to pound the coast.

      The National Weather Service has warned that the rising tides would carry water and waves farther up the beach than usual, making it harder for people to escape from beaches and other coastal areas.

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 10:59 AM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      Tide at San Francisco forecast to approach highest ever recorded

      The National Weather Service said the tide at San Francisco was forecast to approach the highest ever recorded at the city's gauge on Thursday morning, with coastal flooding expected to continue until 4 p.m. Pacific time.

      The National Weather Service had a coastal flood warning in place for shorelines along San Francisco and San Pablo bays, with a lower-level advisory for the Pacific Coast over the same period, warning of up to 2.5 feet of flooding above ground level in low-lying areas.

      The California Governor's Office of Emergency Services has warned residents to "follow local advisories and keep your distance from the shoreline."

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 10:43 AM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for first time ever as storm hits New York

      For the first time in history, Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving parade as heavy rain and strong winds buffet New York.

      The parade will instead take place on Saturday, officials confirmed on Wednesday.

      "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement on Wednesday.

      Officials had been weighing whether the giant balloons could fly safely, and the concern grew after the National Weather Service issued a high-wind warning for the city. The agency said damaging gusts were possible from 10 a.m. Thursday until early Friday, and also forecast moderate to heavy rain.

      New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani acknowledged the "inconvenience" of the rescheduling, but said the move was necessary to protect the safety of participants and spectators.

      "I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," he said. "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first."

      Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency in neighboring New Jersey on Wednesday.

    • Thu, Nov 26, 2026 10:31 AM UTC
      Jasmine Andersson

      What watches, warnings and advisories are in place today?

      Tens of millions of Americans are under weather warnings on Thanksgiving morning, according to the National Weather Service, as storms hit both coasts.

      Coastal flood warnings are covering about 36 million people and high wind warnings are covering about 32 million people as of early Thursday, as a powerful storm hit the East Coast and king tides flooded California.

      Wind advisories alone covered more than 45 million people, the weather service's map shows, largely impacting the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

      A Thanksgiving storm is moving up the East Coast, bringing strong winds, coastal flooding and heavy rain from the Southeast to New England and the Ohio Valley, the Weather Channel reported.

      Wet snow was forecast for parts of the mid-Mississippi Valley, with a rain-snow mix expected across much of the Ohio Valley by Friday.
